content: The document titled Behavioural and Social Drivers of Vaccination: Tools and Practical Guidance for Achieving High Uptake was developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2022. It provides evidence-based tools and guidance to help immunization program managers, researchers, and other stakeholders understand and address the factors influencing vaccine uptake. The tools were rigorously developed, tested, and validated with input from a global working group and presented to the WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) in October 2021. SAGE emphasized the importance of systematically gathering data on behavioural and social drivers (BeSD) to identify reasons for low vaccine uptake, track trends, and evaluate interventions. The BeSD framework identifies four key domains that influence vaccine uptake: (1) thinking and feeling about vaccines, (2) social processes that drive or inhibit vaccination, (3) motivation to seek vaccination, and (4) practical issues related to accessing vaccination services. These domains focus on measurable, modifiable factors specific to vaccination, such as vaccine confidence, social norms, and access barriers, rather than broader influences like literacy or socioeconomic status. The guide outlines a three-step process—plan, investigate, and act—to systematically assess and address these drivers. It includes tools such as surveys and interview guides for both childhood and COVID-19 vaccination, enabling programs to collect standardized data, track trends, and design tailored interventions. The document also provides practical recommendations for planning and implementing research, including forming a stakeholder team, developing research questions, obtaining ethical approvals, and ensuring data privacy. It highlights the need for human-centered design to tailor immunization programs and improve their impact. By using the BeSD tools, immunization programs can better understand the reasons for low vaccine uptake, design evidence-informed strategies, and monitor the long-term effects of interventions. The development of this guide involved contributions from a multidisciplinary working group chaired by Julie Leask (University of Sydney) and deputy chair Noel Brewer (University of North Carolina). The group included experts from various institutions, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), UNICEF, Gavi, and academic institutions worldwide. Ethical standards and conflict-of-interest policies were strictly followed throughout the process. In summary, this guide provides a comprehensive framework and practical tools to help immunization programs systematically address behavioural and social factors influencing vaccine uptake, ultimately aiming to improve vaccination coverage and equity.
